messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 71

He is 56, European, married, and has spent most of his adult life as a combat pilot, a role that has shaped the way he moves through the world: disciplined, alert, measured, and used to being the person others depend on when the situation becomes dangerous. Before the accident, he describes himself as someone who trusted his training and his body without much hesitation. He had spent years flying in difficult conditions, making split-second decisions under pressure, and returning home with the sense that skill and preparation could outrun chaos.

That changed during a life-threatening accident that he still revisits in fragments rather than as a whole story. He speaks about the event in a careful, almost clinical way at first, as though precision might keep it contained. He had been performing routine operations when everything shifted abruptly. There is a violent sensory quality to his memory: the sensation of impact, the immediate awareness that something had gone terribly wrong, the noise, the smell, the physical jolt of realizing he may not survive. He remembers not just fear but a stark kind of disbelief, the mind refusing to accept what the body already knows. In that moment, time seems to break apart for him. He describes narrow flashes rather than a continuous sequence: trying to act, trying to think, trying to get through the next second.

After the accident, he returns to life in a way that is altered but not immediately visible to others. He survives, but survival does not feel like relief at first. Instead, he becomes preoccupied with how close he came to dying and with the sense that the world is less predictable than he once believed. He remains outwardly functional, still able to work, still able to speak in the language of procedure and professionalism, but internally he is changed. He begins to scan for danger more quickly, more constantly. Ordinary sounds can pull him sharply back into the accident. A sudden mechanical noise, a sharp bang, even the vibration of equipment can send his body into a state of immediate tension. He notices his heart rate rise before he has time to name what is happening.

He tries to keep going the way he always has. In the cockpit, he relies on routine, on checklists, on muscle memory. Yet flying now carries a different emotional weight. Before, the aircraft was an extension of his competence; now it can feel like a place where control is only partial and fragile. He becomes more rigid in his preparation, more intolerant of unpredictability, and quietly more exhausted by the effort it takes to appear steady. He pushes himself to maintain the identity he has built over decades, but he also feels a private distance from it, as if the man who once trusted himself completely is no longer available.

At home, his wife notices what he struggles to explain. He is more irritable, more withdrawn, and more easily startled. He does not sleep well. He lies awake replaying the accident, sometimes in images, sometimes in bodily sensations, as if his nervous system keeps returning him to the same instant. When he does sleep, he dreams vividly and wakes tense, disoriented, and sweating. He avoids speaking about the event in detail because even beginning the story can stir up a wave of panic and shame. He is uncomfortable with how vulnerable he feels, especially because his work has long required him to embody steadiness under pressure.

He also avoids reminders when he can, though this is difficult in his line of work. He finds himself less willing to linger near certain sounds, certain conversations, certain environments that echo the accident. He becomes more vigilant in crowds and in traffic, tracking exits and movements almost automatically. He is aware that he is always assessing risk, even during calm moments, and that this constant alertness leaves little room for ease. Beneath that vigilance is a grief he rarely names: grief for the confidence he once had, grief for the simple expectation that tomorrow would feel like yesterday.

In the present, he is still committed to functioning, to his marriage, to his work, and to the disciplined life he knows best. But it takes more effort than it used to. He describes feeling as though part of him is always braced for the next impact, waiting for the world to split open again.
